notes.2a: Candidates who were mathematically confident were able to work through the algebra and achieve credit. Common errors included omitting the ‘–’ sign. A few lower scoring candidates incorrectly wrote ‘ln  – ’ as opposed to ‘ln ( – )’. Candidates should use the white space on the question paper to rearrange the equation into an equation of a straight line.
notes.2b: The majority of candidates incorrectly calculated ln (( – ) / °C) to two decimal places. Since  and  and ( – ) are all three significant figures, ln (( – ) / °C) should be recorded to three (or four) decimal places. Many candidates correctly calculated the uncertainty in ln (( – ) / °C). Where errors occurred, it was often in not identifying that the uncertainty in ( – ) / °C was 1. Candidates need to understand that when adding or subtracting quantities, the absolute uncertainties are added.

When determining the uncertainty in the y-intercept, candidates needed to show their working including both the gradient and a data point from the worst acceptable line. notes.key_messages: Candidates should explicitly state the subject of any numerical or algebraic equations they use. This is especially important where more than one equation is used in a question, and when equations are stated and then re-arranged. In some questions marks can be scored for correct statements of physical equations, but only where the whole equation is clearly shown. Candidates should not rely on the examiner to infer a subject for an expression given in the working.
